_comment: Everything the container needs in order to offer, fetch and install a toolchain.
The dashboard's Tools tab renders it and `bb toolchains` acts on it; adding a toolchain
here is the whole job, as long as it fits one of the five kinds below.
name     what `bb toolchains install|remove` is called with.
probe    where it lands, so the page can tell installed from not: a bare
name is a directory under the toolchain store root, android:<pkg> a package
directory under ANDROID_HOME. System images are not toolchains;
they have a section of their own, above.
platforms  which <os>/<arch> this recipe actually works on. Seven of these
name linux-x86_64 in their URL, and swift names ubuntu24.04, so
"Linux" is not one platform here. `*` in the arch position means
the payload is arch-independent: shell and jars, a git clone, or
a tool that resolves its own platform. An install onto a node
outside the list is refused by name rather than downloading a
couple of hundred megabytes and failing on exec.
requires   other toolchains this one needs in order to work. Installed
first, and only when missing. android-tools drives sdkmanager,
which is a Java program, and without this it failed inside
sdkmanager with a message naming neither Java nor the toolchain
that supplies it.
layout     where this toolchain lands, once, for everybody who needs to
know. `bin` are directories under it to put on PATH, `env` the
variables it sets (valued as a path under it, "" meaning the
toolchain directory itself), `tool` the file whose presence
proves it is installed, and `reports` the name the census
summary calls it. Written here because it was written in four
places (sdk_env_snippet, the agent's STORE_TOOLS and
STORE_PATHS, and sdk_check_one) and they drifted three times
in one day.
A path may start `root:` to mean relative to the store rather
than to this toolchain; the android toolchains share one tree,
since sdkmanager installs into <root>/android whatever the
package is called.
system   the machine's own packages this one needs at runtime, by
package manager: `apt` for the Debian family. A recipe runs
as the job account, so the AGENT installs these first, as
root, on a node it may administer (a managed one); on any
other it names them and carries on, and the tool says which
are missing when it is used. Playwright's browsers are the
case: forty libraries the image gets from install-deps and a
node got from nowhere. An entry may name alternatives,
"libasound2t64|libasound2": a library renamed between
releases, met by whichever is installed and otherwise the
first the machine's repositories carry, since apt refuses a
whole install for one unknown name. tools/check-sysdeps.py
checks every name against each release's package index.
source   how to get it. {dir} is the install directory, {version} whatever
the version resolver returned, {script} a downloaded installer.
kind: tarball      resolve a version, fetch source.url, unpack with strip.
script       fetch source.url and run it with the given args and env.
git          shallow-clone a branch; the tool then updates in place.
command      run something already in the image, pointed at {dir}.
sdkmanager   an android package, installed by sdkmanager.
fresh_only   refuse when the directory already exists, for the recipes that
unpack rather than merge.
verify       run after installing, so a broken unpack fails the install
rather than waiting to fail the first time somebody uses it.
time upstream ships: what a toolchain weighs is measured from the disk once it
is installed, remembered after it is removed, and read from the download's
own Content-Length before that when the URL is the payload itself.
download   how to find out what an install would fetch, for a row that is
not installed yet. Absent means source.url is the payload and
its Content-Length is the answer; "command-urls" runs a dry run
and matches the URLs out of it, which is how playwright's five
bundles and the .NET archive are counted. A recipe that cannot
and the row shows no size until it has been installed once.
No size is written down here. One typed into a file is wrong the next time
upstream ships: a row shows what the toolchain takes on this disk once it is
installed, what it took the last time it was, or what the download weighs
before that. Never a number somebody guessed.
"url-matches" fetches a file upstream publishes and matches the
URLs out of it, which is how rust's three minimal-profile
components are counted; "android-repo" reads sdkmanager's own
index, keyed by the package id an install resolves to; and
"approximate" is a number written down, for the one recipe whose
download cannot be measured before it happens: a git clone has
no content length. It is marked as an approximation everywhere
it is shown.
System images, which are not toolchains. A toolchain is one thing at one
version; a system image exists at every API level at once, and which of
them you want is a question about what you are testing, not about the
catalog. So the flavors live here as data, and the Emulator tab offers an
API level and a flavor rather than a row per flavor that could only
ever install the newest one.
abi      the only one an x86_64 host can run at any speed.
xml      sdkmanager's own index for that flavor: what levels exist,
and what each weighs before it is downloaded.
about    which one to pick, which is the whole question.

google_apis.label: Google APIs
google_apis.about: Google Play services (Maps, sign-in, push) but no Play Store app. Rootable: `adb root` works, which the Play Store images refuse. This is the default, and what bb emu create fetches.

google_apis_playstore.label: Google APIs + Play Store
google_apis_playstore.about: The same, plus the Play Store app itself, for anything that has to sign in to Play, check a license or take an in-app payment. A Play-certified build, so it is not rootable. Google ships it as a separate image; there is no image that is one plus a switch.

android-wear.label: Wear OS
android-wear.about: What modern Galaxy and Pixel watches run. Round screen, tiny API level numbers of its own.

toolchains.name: jdk
toolchains.label: JDK 21 (Temurin)
toolchains.about: A Java runtime for sdkmanager, Gradle and the emulator tooling. The image carries one; a node's toolchain store does not, so this is the first thing a node needs for Android work. On a Mac the same recipe fetches Temurin's macOS build.

toolchains.name: android-tools
toolchains.label: Android command-line tools
toolchains.about: sdkmanager and avdmanager: the bootstrap every other android:* toolchain installs through. The image carries it under /opt/android-sdk; a node installs it here, and its ANDROID_HOME is the store's android/ directory.

run: { command -v unzip >/dev/null 2>&1 && unzip -q "$1" -d "$2"; } || python3 -c "import os,sys,zipfile;z=zipfile.ZipFile(sys.argv[1]);[(z.extract(i,sys.argv[2]), (i.external_attr>>16) and os.chmod(os.path.join(sys.argv[2],i.filename), i.external_attr>>16)) for i in z.infolist()]" "$1" "$2" && root="$(dirname "$2")/android" && mkdir -p "$root/cmdline-tools" && rm -rf "$root/cmdline-tools/latest" && ln -sfn "$2/cmdline-tools" "$root/cmdline-tools/latest"
after: system images and the emulator install through it: bb toolchains install android:emulator, bb emu image add ID

toolchains.name: android:cmake
toolchains.label: Android CMake
toolchains.about: The CMake the NDK's build system uses.

toolchains.name: android:emulator
toolchains.label: Android emulator
toolchains.about: The emulator binary. System images are per API level and come from the image picker above, or from bb emu create on the node. Google ships it for x86_64 Linux only, and the image abi is x86_64 (B278).

toolchains.name: android:platform-tools
toolchains.label: Android platform tools
toolchains.about: adb, and the rest of the tools that talk to a device or an emulator. Every `bb emu` verb goes through adb, so the emulator is unusable without it. Google ships it for x86_64 Linux only, and the image abi is x86_64 (B278).

toolchains.name: android:ndk
toolchains.label: Android NDK
toolchains.about: Native development kit, for C and C++ inside an Android app.

toolchains.name: flutter
toolchains.label: Flutter
toolchains.about: Flutter with the bundled Dart SDK. Builds Android APKs on a Linux node; on a Mac node, with Xcode beside it, the iOS half too.

source.warm_note: warming the toolchain (downloads the bundled dart sdk)

toolchains.name: go
toolchains.label: Go
toolchains.about: Cross-compiles from here to Windows, macOS, Linux and ARM with GOOS and GOARCH: no extra toolchain, no target to install.

toolchains.name: dotnet
toolchains.label: .NET + MAUI
toolchains.about: The .NET SDK plus the maui-android workload: Android apps from C#.

then.note: adding the maui-android workload (android targets from C#)
then.optional: the maui-android workload failed; the plain SDK is still installed

toolchains.name: node
toolchains.label: Node.js
toolchains.about: The JavaScript runtime and npm. Not needed to BE a node (the agent is Python and the provisioner installs that), but a project built with npm needs it here, and so does anything that drives a browser through Playwright.

toolchains.name: playwright
toolchains.label: Playwright browsers
toolchains.about: Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and the playwright module that drives them, together in the store. The image carries a copy of the module and the system libraries; a node carries neither, so the module lands here beside the browsers and NODE_PATH points at it: what bb capture shot and the dashboard's own tests require().

run: npm install --prefix "$1" --no-audit --no-fund --loglevel=error playwright@latest && "$1/node_modules/.bin/playwright" install chromium firefox webkit

toolchains.name: lint-tools
toolchains.label: Lint tools (shellcheck, hadolint, actionlint, ruff, yq, fd)
toolchains.about: What bb lint runs: shellcheck, hadolint, actionlint and ruff, with yq and fd beside them. The image carries all six; a node's store does not, so bb lint on a node skips its checks until this is installed. Static binaries from each project's latest GitHub release.

run: dst="$2/bin"; t="$(mktemp -d)"; mkdir -p "$dst"; cp "$1" "$dst/hadolint"; get() { curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o "$2" "$1"; }; tag() { curl -fsSIL -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' "https://github.com/$1/releases/latest" | sed 's#.*/tag/##'; }; get https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/releases/latest/download/yq_linux_amd64 "$dst/yq"; get https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/releases/latest/download/ruff-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz "$t/ruff.tgz"; tar -xzf "$t/ruff.tgz" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -name ruff -type f | head -1)" "$dst/"; v="$(tag koalaman/shellcheck)"; get "https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/releases/download/$v/shellcheck-$v.linux.x86_64.tar.xz" "$t/sc.txz"; tar -xJf "$t/sc.txz" -C "$t"; cp "$t/shellcheck-$v/shellcheck" "$dst/"; v="$(tag rhysd/actionlint)"; get "https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/releases/download/$v/actionlint_${v#v}_linux_amd64.tar.gz" "$t/al.tgz"; tar -xzf "$t/al.tgz" -C "$t" actionlint; cp "$t/actionlint" "$dst/"; v="$(tag sharkdp/fd)"; get "https://github.com/sharkdp/fd/releases/download/$v/fd-$v-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz" "$t/fd.tgz"; tar -xzf "$t/fd.tgz" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -name fd -type f | head -1)" "$dst/"; chmod +x "$dst"/*; rm -rf "$t"

toolchains.name: ffmpeg
toolchains.label: FFmpeg (video and audio)
toolchains.about: ffmpeg, ffprobe and ffplay, statically built with the codecs a recording actually uses: H.264, H.265, VP9, AV1 and Opus. A Claude session cannot watch a video, so what this is really for is turning one into frames it CAN look at (ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 -vf fps=1 dist/frames/%03d.png), plus the ordinary work of cutting, converting and sizing what a build produced. The image carries ffmpeg for the controller; a node carries nothing until this is installed.

toolchains.name: pytorch
toolchains.label: PyTorch with CUDA (python-ml, numpy, ONNX)
toolchains.about: A Python 3.12 of its own, run as python-ml, with PyTorch built for CUDA (13 as of PyTorch 2.14), numpy, onnx, onnxscript and onnxruntime: what training or running a model on a node's NVIDIA card needs, under bb gpu run. The CUDA libraries come inside PyTorch's wheels, so the node needs only its driver, 580 or newer for CUDA 13; there is no nvcc, which only a custom CUDA kernel would want. On a node without a card it runs on the CPU. A project that needs more packages makes its own environment over it: python-ml -m venv --system-site-packages .venv, then .venv/bin/pip install what it needs, which keeps this one as it was installed. torchrun is beside it. About 6 GB, nearly all of it the CUDA libraries. It works in a folder beside itself on the store, since a node's own disk may not hold the download, and a share that keeps a deleted file while it is still open can leave that folder behind until the next install sweeps it.

run:
dst="$2"; mkdir -p "$dst/bin" "$dst/libexec"; rm -rf "$dst"/.work.* 2>/dev/null || true; t="$(mktemp -d "$dst/.work.XXXXXX")"; tar -xzf "$1" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -name uv -type f | head -1)" "$dst/libexec/uv"; chmod +x "$dst/libexec/uv"; rm -rf "$dst/python"; export UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR="$dst/python" UV_CACHE_DIR="$t/cache" UV_NO_CONFIG=1 UV_LINK_MODE=copy; "$dst/libexec/uv" python install -q 3.12; py="$(find "$dst/python" -path '*/bin/python3.12' -type f | head -1)"; test -x "$py"; "$dst/libexec/uv" pip install -q --python "$py" --break-system-packages torch numpy onnx onnxscript onnxruntime; rel="${py#"$dst"/}"; for n in python-ml torchrun; do if [ "$n" = torchrun ]; then a='-m torch.distributed.run'; else a=''; fi; printf '#!/bin/sh
here="$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")"
exec "$here/../%s" %s "$@"
' "$rel" "$a" > "$dst/bin/$n"; chmod +x "$dst/bin/$n"; done; rm -rf "$t" 2>/dev/null || true
verify: import torch, numpy, onnx; print('torch', torch.__version__, 'cuda', torch.version.cuda)

toolchains.name: graphics
toolchains.label: Graphics tools (ImageMagick, resvg, oxipng, pngquant, cwebp)
toolchains.about: What bb tool graphics runs: ImageMagick's magick for resizing, cropping, composing, annotating and comparing rasters; resvg for SVG to PNG without a browser; oxipng, pngquant and cwebp for what an app ships. A session cannot see a picture it has not rendered, so this is how it makes one it can then read back. Static builds from each project's release; ImageMagick's AppImage is unpacked at install, so nothing here needs FUSE.

run: dst="$2"; bin="$dst/bin"; t="$(mktemp -d)"; mkdir -p "$bin"; get() { curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o "$2" "$1"; }; tag() { curl -fsSIL -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' "https://github.com/$1/releases/latest" | sed 's#.*/tag/##'; }; v="$(tag ImageMagick/ImageMagick)"; im="$t/magick.AppImage"; get "https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/releases/download/$v/ImageMagick-$v-gcc-x86_64.AppImage" "$im"; chmod +x "$im"; (cd "$t" && "$im" --appimage-extract >/dev/null); rm -rf "$dst/magick"; mv "$t/squashfs-root" "$dst/magick"; ln -sf ../magick/AppRun "$bin/magick"; rs="$1"; if ! tar -tzf "$rs" >/dev/null 2>&1; then rs="$t/resvg.tgz"; get https://github.com/linebender/resvg/releases/latest/download/resvg-linux-x86_64.tar.gz "$rs"; fi; tar -xzf "$rs" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -name resvg -type f | head -1)" "$bin/"; v="$(tag oxipng/oxipng)"; get "https://github.com/oxipng/oxipng/releases/download/$v/oxipng-${v#v}-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz" "$t/ox.tgz"; tar -xzf "$t/ox.tgz" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -name oxipng -type f | head -1)" "$bin/"; get https://pngquant.org/pngquant-linux.tar.bz2 "$t/pq.tbz"; python3 -c 'import sys, tarfile; tarfile.open(sys.argv[1]).extractall(sys.argv[2])' "$t/pq.tbz" "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -name pngquant -type f | head -1)" "$bin/"; wv="$(curl -fsS 'https://api.github.com/repos/webmproject/libwebp/tags?per_page=20' | grep -o '"name": *"v[0-9.]*"' | sed 's/.*"v//; s/"//' | sort -V | tail -1)"; get "https://storage.googleapis.com/downloads.webmproject.org/releases/webp/libwebp-$wv-linux-x86-64.tar.gz" "$t/webp.tgz"; tar -xzf "$t/webp.tgz" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -path '*/bin/cwebp' -type f | head -1)" "$(find "$t" -path '*/bin/dwebp' -type f | head -1)" "$bin/"; chmod +x "$bin"/*; rm -rf "$t"

toolchains.name: diagrams
toolchains.label: Diagram renderers (PlantUML, Mermaid)
toolchains.about: What bb tool diagrams runs: PlantUML for UML, sequence and architecture diagrams from text, and Mermaid's command line for the flowcharts and sequence diagrams written in Markdown. A session draws from text and reads the PNG back. PlantUML is one jar and runs on this store's JDK; Mermaid renders through the Chromium the playwright toolchain puts here, so both of those are needed beside this.

run:
dst="$2"; mkdir -p "$dst/bin" "$dst/lib"; cp "$1" "$dst/lib/plantuml.jar"; printf '#!/bin/sh
here="$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")"
exec "${JAVA:-java}" -Djava.awt.headless=true -jar "$here/../lib/plantuml.jar" "$@"
' > "$dst/bin/plantuml"; chmod +x "$dst/bin/plantuml"; npm install --silent --no-audit --no-fund --prefix "$dst" @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli; ln -sf ../node_modules/.bin/mmdc "$dst/bin/mmdc"

toolchains.name: documents
toolchains.label: Document readers (markitdown, PyMuPDF, pandoc)
toolchains.about: What bb tool docs runs: markitdown turns a PDF, a Word document, a slide deck or a spreadsheet into Markdown a session can read, PyMuPDF draws a PDF's pages as pictures for layouts, charts and scans, and pandoc converts between document formats. It also puts a pdftoppm and a pdfinfo on the node, drawn with PyMuPDF, which is what Claude Code's own PDF reader asks for. Their Python is uv's own, kept in this directory, so nothing depends on the machine's. About 650 MB: pandoc is a quarter of it, and markitdown's file-type detector and spreadsheet reader most of the rest.

run:
dst="$2"; t="$(mktemp -d)"; mkdir -p "$dst/bin" "$dst/libexec"; get() { curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o "$2" "$1"; }; tag() { curl -fsSIL -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' "https://github.com/$1/releases/latest" | sed 's#.*/tag/##'; }; tar -xzf "$1" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -name uv -type f | head -1)" "$dst/libexec/uv"; chmod +x "$dst/libexec/uv"; rm -rf "$dst/python" "$dst/venv"; export UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR="$dst/python" UV_CACHE_DIR="$t/cache" UV_NO_CONFIG=1; "$dst/libexec/uv" venv -q --python 3.12 "$dst/venv"; "$dst/libexec/uv" pip install -q --python "$dst/venv/bin/python" 'markitdown[pdf,docx,pptx,xlsx,xls]' pymupdf; ln -sf ../venv/bin/markitdown "$dst/bin/markitdown"; v="$(tag jgm/pandoc)"; get "https://github.com/jgm/pandoc/releases/download/$v/pandoc-$v-linux-amd64.tar.gz" "$t/pandoc.tgz"; tar -xzf "$t/pandoc.tgz" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -path '*/bin/pandoc' -type f | head -1)" "$dst/bin/pandoc"; chmod +x "$dst/bin/pandoc"; test -f "${BB_LIB:-}/poppler.py" || { echo "poppler.py is not beside bb: install this from bb toolchains" >&2; exit 1; }; cp "$BB_LIB/poppler.py" "$dst/libexec/poppler.py"; for n in pdftoppm pdfinfo; do printf '#!/bin/sh
here="$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")"
exec "$here/../venv/bin/python" "$here/../libexec/poppler.py" %s "$@"
' "$n" > "$dst/bin/$n"; chmod +x "$dst/bin/$n"; done; rm -rf "$t"

toolchains.name: office
toolchains.label: LibreOffice, headless
toolchains.about: What bb tool office runs: LibreOffice with no window, to turn a Word document, a slide deck or a spreadsheet into a PDF, and so into pictures of its pages with the documents toolchain, when what it looks like matters and not only what it says. Its AppImage unpacked at install, so nothing here needs FUSE. About 750 MB unpacked.

run: dst="$2"; t="$(mktemp -d)"; mkdir -p "$dst/bin"; cp "$1" "$t/lo.AppImage"; chmod +x "$t/lo.AppImage"; (cd "$t" && ./lo.AppImage --appimage-extract >/dev/null); rm -rf "$dst/lo"; mv "$t/squashfs-root" "$dst/lo"; so="$(find "$dst/lo/opt" -maxdepth 3 -path '*/program/soffice' | head -1)"; test -x "$so"; ln -sf "../${so#"$dst"/}" "$dst/bin/soffice"; rm -rf "$t"

toolchains.name: language-servers
toolchains.label: Language servers (Python, TypeScript)
toolchains.about: What Claude Code's pyright-lsp and typescript-lsp plugins run, so a session sees type errors as it edits instead of at the next build. A session cannot npm install -g into the store, so the servers live here. TypeScript is held at 5, the line typescript-language-server drives; a project's own node_modules copy wins where it has one.

toolchains.name: kotlin-lsp
toolchains.label: Kotlin language server
toolchains.about: What Claude Code's kotlin-lsp plugin runs: JetBrains' standalone Kotlin server, with the Java runtime it needs inside it, from the project's latest release. Named kotlin-lsp the way JetBrains' own Homebrew formula names it.

run: v="$(sed -n 's#.*"tag_name": *"kotlin-lsp/v\([0-9.]*\)".*#\1#p' "$1" | head -1)"; [ -n "$v" ] || { echo 'no kotlin-lsp release named in the answer' >&2; exit 1; }; a=''; [ "$(uname -m)" = aarch64 ] && a='-aarch64'; t="$(mktemp -d)"; curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o "$t/k.tgz" "https://download.jetbrains.com/language-server/kotlin-server/$v/kotlin-server-$v$a.tar.gz"; mkdir -p "$2/server" "$2/bin"; tar -xzf "$t/k.tgz" -C "$2/server" --strip-components=1; ln -sfn ../server/bin/intellij-server "$2/bin/kotlin-lsp"; rm -rf "$t"

toolchains.name: rust
toolchains.label: Rust
toolchains.about: rustup, cargo and the stable toolchain, kept in one directory. A Windows target needs a linker as well: gcc-mingw-w64 via EXTRA_APT_PACKAGES, or zig plus cargo-zigbuild.

after: a Windows target also needs a linker: rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu,
then EXTRA_APT_PACKAGES=gcc-mingw-w64, or bb toolchains install zig + cargo-zigbuild

toolchains.name: swift
toolchains.label: Swift
toolchains.about: The Swift toolchain for Linux: shared logic, server-side Swift, and compiling packages. Not an iOS SDK.

toolchains.name: zig
toolchains.label: Zig
toolchains.about: A C and C++ cross-compiler as much as a language: `zig cc -target x86_64-windows-gnu` turns this box into a Windows toolchain, and it links for Rust too.

toolchains.name: xcodes
toolchains.label: xcodes (Xcode installer)
toolchains.about: The tool that installs and switches Xcode versions on a Mac, from Apple's own downloads: `xcodes install --latest` in a shell on the node, with an Apple ID the first time. Xcode itself is 15GB and Apple's to serve, so it is not a recipe.
